1000.title: SMBv1 Support
1000.description: SMBv1 is an outdated and insecure network protocol with known vulnerabilities, making systems susceptible to attacks like WannaCry. Disabling it significantly reduces the attack surface and improves overall security.Ensure the "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" Windows Optional Feature is disabled. This can be done via PowerShell: `Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol` or through the "Turn Windows features on or off" dialog in Control Panel.

1103.title: Store passwords using reversible encryption
1103.description: Storing passwords using reversible encryption is a major security risk as it allows an attacker who gains access to the system to easily decrypt and retrieve user passwords. This setting should always be disabled.Set the "Store passwords using reversible encryption for all users in the domain" policy to "Disabled" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Account Policies -> Password Policy).

1101.title: Account lockout duration
1101.description: This policy determines how long a locked-out account remains locked before it automatically unlocks. A shorter duration (e.g., 15 minutes) helps prevent denial-of-service attacks by quickly restoring access for legitimate users, while still providing some protection against brute-force attacks.Set the "Account lockout duration" policy to 15 minutes or more in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Account Policies -> Account Lockout Policy).

1100.title: Account lockout threshold
1100.description: This policy specifies the number of failed logon attempts that will cause a user account to be locked out. Setting a threshold (e.g., 10 attempts) helps protect against brute-force password attacks. A setting of "Never" means no lockout, which is highly insecure.Set the "Account lockout threshold" policy to 10 invalid logon attempts or less in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Account Policies -> Account Lockout Policy).

1104.title: Allow Administrator account lockout
1104.description: This policy determines whether the built-in Administrator account can be locked out due to failed logon attempts. While allowing lockout can prevent brute-force attacks against the Administrator, it can also lead to denial of service if it's the only administrative account. It's recommended to allow lockout, but ensure other administrative accounts exist.Set the "Allow Administrator account lockout" policy to "Enabled" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1102.title: Reset account lockout counter
1102.description: This policy defines the time period after which the failed logon attempt counter is reset to zero. A shorter reset time (e.g., 15 minutes), combined with an appropriate lockout duration, helps prevent account lockouts for legitimate users while still deterring brute-force attacks.Set the "Reset account lockout counter after" policy to 15 minutes or more in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Account Policies -> Account Lockout Policy).

1200.title: Access this computer from the network
1200.description: This user right determines which users and groups can connect to the computer from the network. Restricting this right to only necessary administrative accounts (e.g., Administrators) reduces the attack surface and potential for unauthorized network access.Configure the "Access this computer from the network" user right to include only "Administrators" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment). Remove "Everyone", "Users", and "Backup Operators" if they are present.

1201.title: Allow log on locally
1201.description: This user right determines which users and groups can log on directly to the computer's console. Restricting this right to only legitimate users and administrators helps prevent unauthorized physical access.Configure the "Allow log on locally" user right to include "Users" and "Administrators" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment). Remove "Backup Operators" and "Guest" if they are present.

1202.title: Debug programs
1202.description: This user right allows users to attach a debugger to any process or kernel. This is a highly privileged right that can be abused to gain control of the system. It should be restricted to only necessary administrative accounts (e.g., Administrators).Configure the "Debug programs" user right to include only "Administrators" (or remove all if not explicitly needed) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment).

1203.title: Deny access to this computer from the network
1203.description: This user right explicitly prevents specified users and groups from connecting to the computer from the network. Denying network access to guest accounts and local accounts without passwords enhances security by preventing anonymous or easily exploitable network access.Configure the "Deny access to this computer from the network" user right to include "Guests" and "Local account" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment).

1204.title: Deny log on as a batch job
1204.description: This user right prevents specified users and groups from logging on as a batch job. Denying this right to guest accounts prevents them from running scheduled tasks or scripts, which could be exploited for malicious purposes.Configure the "Deny log on as a batch job" user right to include "Guests" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment).

1205.title: Deny log on as a service
1205.description: This user right prevents specified users and groups from logging on as a service. Denying this right to guest accounts prevents them from running services, which could be exploited for privilege escalation or persistent access.Configure the "Deny log on as a service" user right to include "Guests" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment).

1206.title: Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services
1206.description: This user right prevents specified users and groups from logging on via Remote Desktop Services. Denying this right to guest accounts and local accounts without passwords enhances security by preventing unauthorized remote access.Configure the "Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services" user right to include "Guests" and "Local account" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment).

1300.title: Accounts: Block Microsoft accounts
1300.description: This policy controls whether users can add or log on with Microsoft accounts. Blocking Microsoft accounts (setting to 'Users can't add or log on with Microsoft accounts') can be beneficial in corporate environments to enforce local or domain accounts and prevent data synchronization with personal cloud services.Set the "Accounts: Block Microsoft accounts" policy to "Users can't add or log on with Microsoft accounts" (value 3) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1301.title: Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings
1301.description: This policy ensures that the more granular Advanced Audit Policy Configuration settings take precedence over older, broader audit policy categories. This allows for more precise and effective auditing.Set the "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1302.title: Interactive logon: Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL
1302.description: Requiring CTRL+ALT+DEL at logon helps prevent malicious programs from capturing user credentials by ensuring that the logon prompt is legitimate. Disabling this requirement reduces security.Set the "Interactive logon: Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL" policy to "Disabled" (value 0) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1303.title: Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in
1303.description: Displaying the last signed-in user's name can provide information to potential attackers. Disabling this feature enhances privacy and makes it slightly harder for attackers to guess valid usernames.Set the "Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1304.title: Interactive logon: Don't display username at sign-in
1304.description: Similar to not displaying the last signed-in user, not displaying the username at sign-in prevents potential attackers from easily enumerating valid usernames on the system.Set the "Interactive logon: Don't display username at sign-in" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1305.title: Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)
1305.description: This policy requires the client to digitally sign all SMB communications. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks and ensures the integrity and authenticity of network traffic.Set the "Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1306.title: Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)
1306.description: This policy enables the client to digitally sign SMB communications if the server supports it. While "always" signing is preferred, enabling this ensures signing occurs when possible, improving security.Set the "Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1307.title: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)
1307.description: This policy requires the server to digitally sign all SMB communications. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks and ensures the integrity and authenticity of network traffic for clients connecting to this server.Set the "Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1308.title: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (if client agrees)
1308.description: This policy enables the server to digitally sign SMB communications if the client supports it. While "always" signing is preferred, enabling this ensures signing occurs when possible, improving security.Set the "Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (if client agrees)" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1309.title: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts
1309.description: This policy prevents anonymous users from enumerating Security Account Manager (SAM) accounts. This helps prevent attackers from gathering information about valid user accounts, which could be used for brute-force attacks.Set the "Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1310.title: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares
1310.description: This policy prevents anonymous users from enumerating SAM accounts and network shares. This significantly reduces the information an attacker can gather about the system's users and resources.Set the "Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1311.title: Network access: Do not allow storage of passwords and credentials for network authentication
1311.description: This policy prevents the system from storing passwords and credentials for network authentication. This reduces the risk of credentials being compromised if the system is breached.Set the "Network access: Do not allow storage of passwords and credentials for network authentication" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1324.title: Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares
1324.description: This policy restricts anonymous access to named pipes and shares, preventing unauthorized users from accessing system resources or sensitive information.Set the "Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1325.title: Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM
1325.description: This policy restricts which clients can make remote calls to the Security Account Manager (SAM) database. Limiting this access to only administrators prevents unauthorized enumeration of user accounts and other sensitive information.Set the "Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM" policy to "Administrators" (or the specified SDDL string "O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA)") in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1312.title: Network security: Allow LocalSystem NULL session fallback
1312.description: This policy determines whether services running as LocalSystem can fall back to a NULL session when attempting to access network resources. Disabling this prevents potential security vulnerabilities associated with NULL sessions.Set the "Network security: Allow LocalSystem NULL session fallback" policy to "Disabled" (value 0) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1326.title: Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change
1326.description: This policy prevents the storage of LAN Manager (LM) hash values, which are weak and easily crackable. Disabling LM hash storage significantly improves password security.Set the "Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1313.title: Network security: LAN Manager authentication level
1313.description: This policy controls the authentication protocol used for network logons. Setting it to "Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM" (level 5) ensures the use of the strongest available NTLM protocol, preventing the use of weaker, vulnerable protocols.Set the "Network security: LAN Manager authentication level" policy to "Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM" (value 5) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1314.title: Network security: LDAP client signing requirements
1314.description: This policy enforces LDAP client signing, which helps prevent man-in-the-middle attacks and ensures the integrity and authenticity of LDAP communications.Set the "Network security: LDAP client signing requirements" policy to "Negotiate signing" (value 1) or "Require signing" (value 2) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1315.title: Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) clients
1315.description: This policy enforces minimum security requirements for NTLM SSP-based client sessions, such as requiring NTLMv2 session security and 128-bit encryption. This strengthens the security of NTLM communications.Set the "Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) clients" policy to "Require NTLMv2 session security" and "Require 128-bit encryption" (value 537395200) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1316.title: Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) servers
1316.description: This policy enforces minimum security requirements for NTLM SSP-based server sessions, such as requiring NTLMv2 session security and 128-bit encryption. This strengthens the security of NTLM communications for servers.Set the "Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) servers" policy to "Require NTLMv2 session security" and "Require 128-bit encryption" (value 537395200) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1317.title: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic
1317.description: This policy audits incoming NTLM traffic, helping to identify systems or applications still using the less secure NTLM protocol. Auditing is a crucial step before restricting NTLM.Set the "Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic" policy to "Enable auditing for all accounts" (value 2) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1318.title: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain
1318.description: This policy audits NTLM authentication attempts within the domain, providing visibility into NTLM usage. This is essential for planning the eventual restriction or disabling of NTLM.Set the "Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain" policy to "Enable auditing for domain accounts to domain servers" (value 7) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1319.title: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers
1319.description: This policy restricts outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers, preventing the system from sending NTLM credentials to potentially untrusted or insecure remote systems.Set the "Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers" policy to "Deny all" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1320.title: Shutdown: Allow system to be shut down without having to log on
1320.description: Allowing shutdown without logon can lead to denial-of-service attacks or unauthorized system restarts. Requiring logon ensures that only authorized users can shut down the system.Set the "Shutdown: Allow system to be shut down without having to log on" policy to "Disabled" (value 0) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1321.title: User Account Control: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account
1321.description: Enabling Admin Approval Mode for the built-in Administrator account ensures that even the Administrator runs with standard user privileges by default, requiring explicit elevation for administrative tasks. This reduces the risk of malware running with full administrative rights.Set the "User Account Control: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account" policy to "Enabled" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1322.title: User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode
1322.description: This policy controls how UAC elevation prompts behave for administrators. Setting it to "Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop" (value 2) provides the highest level of security by requiring a username and password on a secure desktop, preventing malware from interacting with the prompt.Set the "User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode" policy to "Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop" (value 2) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1323.title: User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users
1323.description: This policy controls how UAC elevation prompts behave for standard users. Setting it to "Prompt for credentials" (value 1) or "Automatically deny elevation requests" (value 0) ensures that standard users cannot perform administrative tasks without explicit administrator credentials or are simply denied.Set the "User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users" policy to "Prompt for credentials" (value 1) or "Automatically deny elevation requests" (value 0) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options).

1400.title: EnableFirewall (Domain Profile, Policy)
1400.description: The Windows Firewall should be enabled for the Domain Profile to protect the system from unauthorized network access when connected to a domain network. This ensures that only explicitly allowed traffic can communicate with the system.Set the "Windows Firewall: Domain Profile: State" policy to "On (recommended)" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Domain Profile).

1418.title: EnableFirewall (Domain Profile)
1418.description: The Windows Firewall should be enabled for the Domain Profile to protect the system from unauthorized network access when connected to a domain network. This ensures that only explicitly allowed traffic can communicate with the system.Enable the Windows Firewall for the Domain Profile via "Windows Firewall with Advanced Security" (wf.msc) or Local Security Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Windows Firewall with Advanced Security -> Windows Firewall Properties -> Domain Profile).

1401.title: Inbound Connections (Domain Profile, Policy)
1401.description: The default behavior for inbound connections in the Domain Profile should be to block all connections that are not explicitly allowed by a firewall rule. This is a fundamental security practice to prevent unauthorized access.Set the "Windows Firewall: Domain Profile: Inbound connections" policy to "Block (default)" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Domain Profile).

1402.title: Outbound Connections (Domain Profile, Policy)

This is the standard configuration for most environments, balancing security with functionality.Set the "Windows Firewall: Domain Profile: Outbound connections" policy to "Allow (default)" in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Domain Profile).

1403.title: Log size limit (Domain Profile, Policy)
1403.description: Increasing the log file size for the Windows Firewall Domain Profile ensures that more historical data on network activity is retained. This is crucial for security auditing, incident response, and troubleshooting.Set the "Windows Firewall: Domain Profile: Logging: Size limit (KB)" policy to 16384 KB or higher in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Domain Profile -> Logging).

1404.title: Log dropped packets (Domain Profile, Policy)

This is crucial for security auditing, incident response, and troubleshooting.Set the "Windows Firewall: Public Profile: Logging: Size limit (KB)" policy to 16384 KB or higher in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Public Profile -> Logging).

1433.title: Log size limit (Public Profile)

This is crucial for security auditing, incident response, and troubleshooting.Set the "Log file size (KB)" setting for the Public Profile to 16384 KB or higher via "Windows Firewall with Advanced Security" (wf.msc) or Local Security Policy (Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Windows Firewall with Advanced Security -> Windows Firewall Properties -> Public Profile -> Logging).

1416.title: Log dropped packets (Public Profile, Policy)
1416.description: Enabling logging of dropped packets for the Windows Firewall Public Profile provides valuable information about blocked network attempts, which can indicate potential attacks or misconfigurations.Set the "Windows Firewall: Public Profile: Logging: Log dropped packets" policy to "Yes" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Public Profile -> Logging).

1434.title: Log dropped packets (Public Profile)

1417.title: Log successful connections (Public Profile, Policy)

This is useful for security monitoring and compliance.Set the "Windows Firewall: Public Profile: Logging: Log successful connections" policy to "Yes" (value 1) in Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> Network Connections -> Windows Firewall -> Public Profile -> Logging).

1435.title: Log successful connections (Public Profile)
